question: Does the within-model activation-ratio -> causal-damage relation found in a genomic decoder reproduce in a TEXT decoder, and is it graded or threshold-like?
design: 36 rows log-spaced by activation-ratio RANK inside ONE layer of ONE model; each ablated to alpha=0 (epsilon=1.0); native LM NLL on that model's frozen census eval pool. Row selection by activation ratio only, never by causal outcome. Identical logic in both models.

statistic_provenance.prespecified: rho(all rows), rho(excl. frozen candidate), rho(ratio<5) -- fixed before the run
statistic_provenance.posthoc: rho(ratio>=5) and rho(ratio>=5, excl. candidate) -- added after seeing the scatter. The split point is the detector's own pre-existing >=5 accept rule and was NOT fitted to these data, but the decision to decompose by regime was made post hoc.

finding: Two-regime, replicated in both domains. BELOW the detector threshold the ratio carries no positive graded signal (genomic rho=+0.040 p=0.86; text rho=-0.584 p=0.005, i.e. mildly INVERTED). ABOVE it the ratio grades severity strongly (genomic rho=+0.639 p=0.010; text rho=+0.975 p=7.1e-10), and survives removing the frozen candidate (+0.556 / +0.969). The mediocre pooled rho reported earlier (+0.454 genomic) is a dilution artifact of averaging a noise regime with a graded one.
caveats: one layer and one candidate per model

sub-threshold rel_delta magnitudes are ~1e-5, ~1e3x above the harness's float reproducibility (baseline reproduced to 1.5e-8 rel) but physically negligible -- the negative text correlation is a real ordering of trivial effects, not a mechanism
supra/sub decomposition is post hoc (see statistic_provenance)
